title: Multiple Modules
story: Your app now has math functions, string helpers, user models, and validation logic. One module isn't enough. You need separate modules — each with a clear purpose — that work together. Let's organize a real app with multiple cooperating modules.
why: Real applications use multiple modules to separate concerns — data models, business logic, utilities, and display code each get their own namespace, making the codebase navigable and maintainable.
analogy: Multiple modules are like departments in a company — Accounting (models) manages data, Legal (validation) checks rules, Marketing (display) handles presentation, and Management (app) coordinates them all. Each department has its own expertise and doesn't meddle in the others' work.
try_it: Add a `tax` module that calculates 8% sales tax. Modify `store.sell_item` to apply both discount AND tax (discount first, then tax on the discounted price). Add a `receipt` module that prints a formatted receipt showing item name, original price, discount amount, tax, and final total. Each module should only do ONE thing.
tips: Leaf modules (models, validation) should NOT import from orchestrator modules — dependencies flow one direction
Each module should have one clear purpose — if you can describe a module in 3 words, it's well-scoped
Module names document the architecture: `models`, `validation`, `display` tell you the concern at a glance
common_mistakes: Creating circular dependencies: module A uses module B, which uses module A — this creates confusion; keep dependencies one-directional
Putting everything in one module — 'utils' or 'helpers' with 50 functions is not a module, it's a dumping ground
Accessing private items across modules — `models.User` is only accessible if `User` is marked `pub`
